seasons.review_body: Series 1 premiered on BBC One in April 2018, written by Abi Morgan, and earned 74% on Rotten Tomatoes with a 72 Metacritic score. Critics found the show's central conceit - a family of divorce lawyers whose own family is fracturing - dramatically rich if occasionally too neatly assembled. Paste Magazine praised the show when it allowed the Defoe women to 'face real decisions and consequences'. The Independent called the sibling dynamic 'a delight, realistically but warmly observed'. Nicola Walker's Hannah established immediately as a performance of controlled emotional precision, and her chemistry with Stephen Mangan as husband Nathan anchored a marriage the show would spend three series slowly and deliberately dismantling. The Times noted the show was 'often too polished for its own good' while acknowledging its pleasures.

# The Split S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A father tells his daughter she is being sent away, and the premiere never leaves that room for long. Years later, **Hannah Stern** works in settlements, visitation, offers, retractions, Wednesdays. The vocabulary has improved. The wound has not. The sharpest idea in The Split's opening hour is simple: control looks professional until it gets personal, then it repeats old mistakes in better clothes. This is a sturdy, dialogue-heavy premiere that finds its best drama when legal strategy starts sounding like family history.

## Control Is the First Lie

The boarding-school opening gives the hour its private grammar. Hannah's father announces separation as policy. No debate. No warmth. No gradual preparation. A decision is made, and a child is informed. The episode later moves into divorce negotiations and visitation arguments, but that first scene matters because it defines how this world uses procedure. Procedure can be care. It can also be punishment in a neater font.

Hannah's adult mode is command. She wants the divorce and visitation process kept moving, and her instinct is clear: give the divorce the best advice and keep the settlement on track. The hour frames that instinct through information management too. When the line "I think they already suspect" hangs over the question of who knows what, Hannah tries to manage the leak before it becomes a flood.

That makes her early declaration land harder. Hannah says, "I just don't love you any more." It is blunt, almost legally clean in its finality. The writing does not decorate it. It lets the sentence sit there as a verdict pretending to be a confession. In this universe, people do not always lose control by shouting. Sometimes they lose it by reducing a life to a sentence they can survive saying out loud.

## The Tweets Turn Custody into Ammunition

The divorce case gives the premiere its most efficient engine. **Rex** wants time with his son. Counsel warns against making threats with visitation. The proposed fix is absurdly modern and plausible inside the episode's logic: cut the tweets, and maybe he gets Wednesdays back. A public grievance has become a bargaining chip. The captioned insult about an ex-wife shows how fast private collapse becomes content.

This is where the legal dialogue works best. The stakes are specific enough to hurt. Wednesdays matter because they are not abstract custody language. They are a recurring slot in a child's life. The proposed weekend extension matters because it sounds negotiable until a parent hears it as a loss. The episode is strongest when it makes the law feel like a calendar. Who gets which night? Who gets punished for which sentence? What has to be deleted before access returns?

**Sarah** becomes the necessary counterweight. She wants to prevent punitive or irrational divorce terms and protect the child's time. That is a clean dramatic function, and the episode gives her enough friction to matter. She does not simply accept the modified visitation terms. She escalates later at the party, which keeps her from becoming the sensible person who exists only to say the healthiest option out loud.

Rex is still more pressure point than full person in this opening hour. His lack of control in the office confrontation and his later presence in the square are useful beats, but the full reason he is prevented from seeing Eddie remains an open loop. That may pay off later. Here, it keeps part of the custody story slightly procedural when it is reaching for personal heat.

## Hannah Breaks the Deal She Is Supposed to Protect

The premiere's best turn is Hannah's contradiction in motion. She is positioned as the person who can keep the settlement alive, but under conflict she retracts the offer of every Wednesday night and refuses the current visitation shape. That is the hour's argument in one action. Hannah does not fail because she lacks intelligence. She fails because she trusts control more than process.

That distinction matters. The writing places her inside a system where language can soften or sharpen harm. "Desist with tweets" is an action. "Might get him his Wednesdays back" is leverage. "Do not make threats with visitation" is advice and warning. Hannah hears all of this, understands all of this, and still reaches for the tool she knows will hurt. The irony is blunt, but divorce drama can bear bluntness. People keep saying they want the child's best interest while grabbing the nearest weapon.

There is a nice brutality in how the show handles competence. Hannah can speak well. She can reassert terms after conflict. She can survive a room full of difficult adults. None of that saves her from repeating the shape of the first scene. A powerful person decides. Someone else absorbs the consequence.

The pacing helps. Dialogue density rises around the negotiation turns, and that density suits the material. The scenes sound like people trying to win with syntax. Then the gaps and silences around them let the pressure sit. Words do the damage. The quiet afterward shows the bruise.

## Nina Arrives Like a Warning

**Nina** enters with a simple greeting to Hannah, but her function is messier than the hello suggests. She wants to stay in communication and help coordinate support. Then she does not arrive as expected and signals she has a party to go to. That small contradiction gives the episode another version of its main idea. Everyone says they are managing the situation. Everyone has somewhere else the situation spills.

The father material deepens this without a speech. Hannah is told that a father went out to buy a newspaper and never came back. The line echoes the opening boarding-school decision without copying it. One absence is formal and announced. One is casual and devastating. Placed near Hannah's professional life, the connection is clear: abandonment teaches people to prize control, and control makes them dangerous in rooms where flexibility might save them.

The restraint helps. The episode does not turn the father thread into an instant emotional explosion. It plants the detail and lets Hannah keep moving. That fits her better than a breakdown would. Hannah's survival strategy is motion, advice, terms, speeches, reassertion. The wound stays active because she refuses to stop long enough to look at it.

This strand still carries some first-episode stiffness. Nina's missed arrival and party signal are useful, but they also read as positioning for a wider family mesh. The beat works as a warning. It has not yet become a full charge. For a premiere, that is acceptable. It plants enough to make the family side feel like more than decoration around the casework.

## Cake, Panic, and the Speech That Has to Hold

The party sequence brings the hour's public and private languages into the same room. Hannah panics with the line, "Oh, shit. Cake." It is funny because it is small. After legal threats, visitation damage, father wounds, and emotional retractions, cake becomes the immediate crisis. The specificity is the joke, and the joke pays rent because it shows Hannah's brain snapping back to logistics. When feeling becomes too much, find the next task.

The speech that follows matters because Hannah reasserts terms after conflict. The episode does not use the party as a soft landing. It uses it as another arena. Sarah escalates there. Nina's coordination wobbles around it. Rex is present in the square. The public setting turns private settlement into social theatre, and Hannah must perform steadiness while her own choices have made the ground less steady.

That is the premiere's craft pattern: put Hannah in rooms where she can sound in control, then make the room reveal what control has cost. Sometimes the device is legal language. Sometimes it is family history. Sometimes it is cake. The stronger scenes understand that these are connected. For Hannah, the divorce table and the party table are linked by the same fear. If she stops directing traffic, someone disappears, someone takes the child, someone changes the terms.

The episode would be sharper if a few secondary beats carried more texture on arrival. Rex, Eddie, and the modified-material question remain partly held back. But the central construction is solid. The premiere builds Hannah as capable, wounded, and capable of wound-making. That is enough to open the case.

## The Verdict

The Split's first episode is a solid, intelligent premiere with one clean spine: divorce procedure becomes dangerous when the people using it mistake control for care. Hannah is the hour's strongest asset because the writing lets her be professionally fluent and personally reckless in the same breath. The custody and tweet negotiations give the episode a sharp contemporary mechanism, while the father material gives it an older bruise. The weakness is some launch-episode scaffolding, especially around Rex and the still-withheld Eddie question, which keeps one side of the conflict thinner than the other. Even so, the hour earns its place as an opener. It plants legal stakes, family damage, and Hannah's central contradiction without pretending they will stay tidy.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The S1 finale earned an 88% Rotten Tomatoes audience score and closed the Hannah-Nathan strand with emotional restraint. Den of Geek praised the premiere episode highly, and the finale paid off on those character investments across six episodes. Nicola Walker and Stephen Mangan's performances were the central element singled out in season reviews, and the finale let both actors play the resolution without over-dramatizing it.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 improved to 78% on Rotten Tomatoes as the Hannah-Nathan marriage tension deepened and the show's family firm dynamics grew more entangled and dramatically productive.

pull_quotes.text: Walker and Mangan are still great at understated comedy and digging out emotional truths.

seasons.review_body: Series 2 aired in February-March 2020 and earned 78% on Rotten Tomatoes. Critics noted an improvement in the show's confidence - the Walker-Mangan central dynamic had deepened into something more complex and less polished than the debut season's surface-sheen. The Telegraph praised both leads for their 'understated comedy and emotional truth'. The Wall Street Journal, after initial reservations, noted the show found 'its footing as powerful drama' once its wandering subplots resolved. The family firm subplot - with Fiona Button and Annabel Scholey as Hannah's sisters - generated the most praised ensemble scenes of the series, and Deborah Findlay as matriarch Ruth provided the emotional backbone that held the family dynamics together.
seasons.season_over_season: A step up from Season 1 - the Hannah-Nathan marriage unravels with more complexity and less polish than the debut.

bollymeter.basis: The concluding series resolved Hannah and Nathan's arc to broadly positive critical reception - audiences who had invested three seasons found the emotional payoff handled with the quiet intelligence the series had developed.

seasons.review_body: Series 3 aired April-May 2022 as the main narrative conclusion of The Split, bringing Hannah and Nathan's long-running marital dissolution to a resolution the show had earned through three seasons of patient character work. Abi Morgan's writing had by Series 3 moved past the show's early reputation as glossy BBC drama - the audience consensus of 91% on Rotten Tomatoes overall reflected an investment that deepened with each series. The three-season arc demonstrated something rare: a drama whose understanding of its characters genuinely sharpened over time, allowing Nicola Walker and Stephen Mangan to deliver performances of increasing subtlety. The December 2024 two-part special provided a coda for those who wanted further resolution.
seasons.season_over_season: The strongest entry in dramatic terms - three seasons of careful character investment pay off in the concluding episodes.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series finale wrapped three seasons of legal and marital drama with more honesty than resolution. The show understood that separation is rarely clean, and the final episode gave each major character a landing that felt true to who they had become. The Rotten Tomatoes critical consensus for S3 held at 100% on a small but unanimously positive critical sample. A two-part special in December 2024 revisited the characters.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Hannah's final decision - delivered not as a dramatic announcement but as an ordinary conversation, which made it land harder.
